screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, study-design, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of queue positions 1-12 after Batch 05 publication.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Effect of a 90-Minute Nap at Different Times of the Day on Physical Performance, Psycho-Cognitive Responses, and Perceived Recovery in Trained Youth Male Athletes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Fourteen trained male athletes aged 18 plus or minus 1 year completed four randomized crossover conditions comparing no nap with a 90-minute nap beginning at 13:00 or 15:00. The 13:00 nap produced greater total shuttle-run distance than the 15:00 nap and 15:00 no-nap condition, greater best distance than both no-nap conditions, and better digit-cancelation performance, while fatigue index, feeling state, and Hooper scores did not differ.
records.limitations: The sample was small, male, young, and trained; only one nap duration and one intermittent shuttle protocol were tested. Chronotype and individual sleep need were not used to personalize the nap, and standardized post-nap light and television exposure may have affected responses.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat the result as a promising timing-specific crossover finding rather than a universal 90-minute nap prescription; the later nap was not equivalent and the study does not establish effects in female athletes, other ages, or other performance tasks.

records.sourceFile: Relationship between training load and recovery in collegiate American football players during pre-season training.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Seventeen collegiate American football players were monitored across a 14-day preseason using accelerometry, heart rate, session RPE, next-day reactive strength index, and perceived recovery. Higher session-RPE load predicted lower next-day reactive strength index, while higher mechanical load predicted lower perceived recovery; relationships differed by position group and changed between weeks.
records.limitations: The study included only 17 athletes from one program, with six linemen and 11 non-linemen after seven monitored players were excluded because of injury. The observation window covered only 14 preseason days, so estimates may not transfer across a full season or other programs.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the measures as complementary signals within an individual and position-aware monitoring process, not as universal thresholds or evidence that one load metric alone determines readiness.

records.sourceFile: Decreased isometric neck strength is a risk factor for head  neck and face injuries in professional rugby league players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Thirty-two male professional rugby league players completed preseason cervical strength, endurance, and proprioception testing and were followed for head, neck, and face injuries causing missed games. Weaker neck extensors below the study cut points and left-to-right lateral-flexor asymmetry were associated with substantially greater unadjusted injury odds.
records.limitations: This exploratory prospective study used a convenience sample from one professional team, produced wide confidence intervals, was underpowered for some strength variables, and did not adjust for multiple comparisons or key exposure and collision covariates.
records.synthesisCaution: The reported cut points are team-specific hypothesis-generating values, not validated clinical thresholds; association does not prove that increasing strength or symmetry will prevent head, neck, or face injury.

records.sourceFile: Effect of training day match and length of the microcycle on the worst-case scenarios in professional soccer players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-three Spanish second-division players were observed across 43 training sessions and 13 matches. Rolling worst-case distance, high-speed-running, and sprinting demands over 1-, 3-, 5-, and 10-minute windows were highest in matches; the largest training values generally occurred four or three days before the match and one day after, with training-day values also varying by microcycle length.
records.limitations: The analysis came from one team and four mesocycles, excluded goalkeepers and incomplete sessions, and was constrained by GPS measurement error and limited comparable worst-case-scenario literature. It did not test whether prescribing drills from these observations improves performance or reduces injury.
records.synthesisCaution: Use rolling peak-demand profiles to inform drill design and weekly exposure, but avoid copying the reported values across teams, devices, positions, or age groups without local calibration.

records.sourceFile: Effects of an 8-week pre-season targeted training on sprinting performance, agility and lower limb muscular asymmetries in elite soccer players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Thirty-two elite soccer players were randomized to control or an eight-week preseason program adding four weekly sessions of six unilateral bodyweight exercises. The experimental group improved 5-m and 30-m sprint and change-of-direction performance, with changes in measured muscle activation and partial reductions in lower-limb asymmetry.
records.limitations: The small single-context sample and bundled intervention prevent identifying which exercise or training component caused the changes. Surface-EMG garments estimate activation rather than force, and the study did not prospectively test injury incidence despite discussing injury-risk implications.
records.synthesisCaution: Interpret the intervention as a combined preseason movement-pattern program with performance outcomes; do not infer that EMG asymmetry correction alone caused improvement or that the program prevents injury.

records.sourceFile: Return to play performance and career duration after ACL rupture - A case control study in the five biggest football nations in Europe.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A five-year media-based case-control study identified 132 ACL ruptures in 125 male players from the top two leagues of England, Spain, Italy, Germany, and France and matched each injured player with two controls. Although 98.2% returned to play, only 59.4% returned at the same level; career survival and several match-performance indicators remained lower than in controls.
records.limitations: Injuries, procedures, and participation were reconstructed from validated public media databases rather than clinical records. Side, surgical technique, rehabilitation exposure, symptoms, and non-time-loss history were unavailable, and residual differences between cases and matched controls may remain.
records.synthesisCaution: A high binary return-to-play rate should not be interpreted as full restoration of competitive level, performance, or career longevity, and these historical European professional-soccer estimates are not individual prognoses.

records.sourceFile: Reconsidering Exercise Selection with EMG - Poor Agreement between Ranking Hip Exercises with Gluteal EMG and Muscle Force.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Fourteen healthy female footballers performed eight hip-focused exercises while kinematics, forces, and surface EMG informed a neuromusculoskeletal model. Exercise rankings based on gluteal EMG and estimated force agreed weakly, and EMG alone explained little between-exercise force variation, although relationships strengthened after accounting for exercise- and participant-specific effects.
records.limitations: The small female-only sample and eight tested exercises limit generalization. Model-estimated muscle forces were not directly validated in vivo, muscle-tendon parameters were not fully personalized, and both EMG and modeling remain proxy measures rather than longitudinal adaptation outcomes.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not rank dissimilar exercises or prescribe loading from peak EMG alone; within-athlete and biomechanically comparable contrasts may be more informative, but exercise selection still requires task, load, range, tolerance, and progression context.

records.sourceFile: The Application of Blood Flow        Restriction- Lessons From the Laboratory.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This laboratory-to-practice narrative review summarized blood-flow-restriction methods across low-load resistance, aerobic, disuse, rehabilitation, and athletic contexts. It emphasized that cuff width, material, limb size, and individual arterial occlusion pressure alter the applied stimulus and recommended individualized relative pressure rather than one absolute pressure for everyone.
records.limitations: The article was a narrative methods review rather than a systematic review or comparative clinical trial. Safety and effectiveness evidence varied across populations and protocols, while practical elastic wrapping lacked validated dosing across diverse patients and left vascular effects uncertain.
records.synthesisCaution: Blood-flow restriction requires trained clinical oversight, appropriate screening, individualized pressure and cuff selection, and symptom monitoring; the review does not support improvised or uniform-pressure application.

records.sourceFile: The effect of the Copenhagen Adduction and Nordic Hamstring exercises on muscle strength and athletic performance - A quasi-experimental study.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Thirty-eight adolescent male soccer players completed a four-week preseason program combining Nordic hamstring and Copenhagen adduction exercises twice weekly. Isometric hamstring strength increased by about 11% and eccentric adduction strength by about 17%, while jump performance declined and sprint changes were small and not consistently significant.
records.limitations: The quasi-experimental pre-post design lacked a control group and randomization, had substantial loss to follow-up across separate testing occasions, and was embedded in normal preseason training. These features weaken causal attribution and may have obscured performance effects.
records.synthesisCaution: The combined exercises appear useful for targeted strength development, but do not assume transfer to sprint or jump performance or injury prevention from this short uncontrolled study.

records.sourceFile: Acute and post-acute COVID-19 presentations in athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review and meta-analysis included 43 observational studies and 11,518 athletes. About 94% had mild or no acute symptoms, the pooled persistent-symptom estimate was 8.3%, and myocardial-involvement estimates varied by testing strategy; controlled studies did not establish that COVID-19 caused the cardiac findings.
records.limitations: Included studies were heterogeneous in athlete selection, testing, symptom definitions, follow-up, and risk of bias, with substantial uncertainty around pooled estimates. Serial assessment was limited, and myocardial abnormalities were not consistently linked to symptoms, controls, or clinical consequences.
records.synthesisCaution: Population averages cannot replace individual clinical assessment; persistent symptoms should influence graded return timing, while incidental imaging findings should not be presented as proven COVID-19 injury without appropriate comparison and interpretation.

records.sourceFile: Acute effects of cluster and rest redistribution set structures on mechanical, metabolic, and perceptual fatigue during and after resistance training - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 32 studies found that cluster and rest-redistribution structures generally preserved repetition velocity and power, reduced within-session mechanical decline, lactate accumulation, and perceived exertion compared with traditional sets. Cluster sets often showed larger effects, partly because they commonly added more total rest.
records.limitations: Protocols varied in load, repetitions, proximity to failure, total rest, exercise, training status, and outcome definitions, producing heterogeneity. Cluster and rest-redistribution comparisons were not always work-rest matched, and available studies primarily addressed acute responses rather than long-term adaptation.
records.synthesisCaution: Use alternative set structures when maintaining movement quality or limiting acute fatigue is the session goal, but account for total rest and do not assume superior chronic strength or hypertrophy without longitudinal evidence.

records.sourceFile: Acute effects of overspeed stimuli with towing system on athletic sprint performance - A systematic review with meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review and meta-analysis combined 16 studies with 296 participants aged 14-31 years. Towing-assisted overspeed conditions acutely increased maximum running speed and stride length and reduced contact time, but force and EMG findings were insufficient to distinguish athlete-generated changes from direct assistance by the device.
records.limitations: Studies used varied towing devices, loads, populations, sprint protocols, and biomechanical measures, with limited elite-sprinter data. The review concerned acute assisted sprint responses and included too little consistent force or EMG evidence to identify mechanism or establish long-term training benefit.
records.synthesisCaution: An immediate faster assisted sprint is not evidence of retained unassisted speed; individualize and quantify assistance, monitor mechanics, and evaluate transfer over repeated training before treating overspeed towing as effective.
